content: Dyspepsia occurs in approximately 3% of cases, while hypersensitivity to rifamycin or other rifamycin-class antimicrobial agents is reported in less than 2% of cases. Rifamycin is not effective for diarrhea that is complicated by fever and/or bloody stools. If diarrhea worsens or persists for more than 48 hours, the medication should be discontinued, and alternative antibacterial therapy should be considered. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following the use of antibacterial drugs, as CDAD can occur up to two months after discontinuing antibiotics. Prescribing rifamycin without a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection, or without a prophylactic indication, is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Due to the minimal systemic concentrations of rifamycin observed, clinically significant drug interactions are not expected. There is no available data regarding the use of rifamycin in pregnant women. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child or from the underlying maternal condition. Rifamycin is generally considered acceptable for use, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. Approximately 1% of the drug is protein-bound, and CYP-based metabolism has not been observed in vitro. The drug is primarily excreted in the feces, with 86% eliminated through this route. Each dose should be taken with a full glass of liquid (6–8 ounces) and should not be taken concurrently with alcohol. Rifamycin may be taken with or without food. Delayed-release tablets should be swallowed whole and not crushed, broken, or chewed. The medication should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted between 15–30°C (59–86°F).
